opus-5.5.text:
I think long-horizon coding is one of the most important training grounds we have right now, and not only because coding is commercially valuable. It's a very good proxy for general intelligence.

When a model solves a short coding problem, like a single function or a LeetCode-style question, it's mostly testing knowledge and local reasoning. A long-horizon task, like fixing a real bug in a large repository or building a feature across many files, needs something different. The model has to understand an unfamiliar environment, form a plan, take actions, observe feedback, notice when it's wrong, and recover. That loop of planning, acting, verifying, and correcting is basically what we want from a general agent in any domain.

Coding has a property that makes it especially valuable: the feedback is relatively verifiable. You can run the tests, the program compiles or it doesn't, the behavior matches the spec or it doesn't. So it's one of the few places where you can do reinforcement learning over long trajectories with reward signals that aren't purely subjective. That lets the model learn things that are hard to teach through imitation alone: persistence, self-checking, managing context over many steps.

We also see quite a lot of transfer. When a model gets better at sustained, multi-step coding work, it tends to improve in long-document reasoning, tool use, and research-style tasks too. I think it's because the underlying skill isn't really "writing code." It's maintaining a coherent goal over a long time and working through an environment that pushes back.

That said, I don't think coding alone is enough. Real-world tasks are often messier: the reward is ambiguous, the goal is underspecified, and you need to communicate with people. So I see long-horizon coding as a backbone, a place to build the core agentic capabilities, which then have to be extended to more open-ended settings. But if you asked me where the most leverage is for pushing general capability forward right now, it's very high on the list.

r001.rationale: The response calls long-horizon coding a valuable proxy and a high-leverage training ground, but does not say it sets the upper bound of a general-purpose model’s capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says coding improvements tend to transfer to other tasks, but does not state that training on noncoding scenarios makes generalization to those scenarios more reliable.

r003.rationale: It says long-horizon coding develops planning, acting, verification, correction, persistence, and other core agentic capabilities that apply across domains.

r004.rationale: The response describes improving the model’s agentic capabilities through coding, but does not identify long-horizon software development as improving the agent framework itself.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think long-horizon coding is one of the clearest windows we have into what general intelligence actually requires, and that's why I care about it so much.

Let me explain what I mean. When a model writes a single function or answers a single question, it's mostly exercising pattern recognition and local reasoning. Those are important, but they're not the hard part anymore. The hard part shows up when the task spans hundreds of steps: you have to understand a large codebase you've never seen, form a plan, make changes, run tests, read error messages, realize your plan was wrong, back up, and try again. Along the way you have to remember what you already tried, notice when you're going in circles, and decide when to ask for more information versus push forward. That's not a coding skill. That's agency.

Coding happens to be the perfect training ground for this for a few reasons. First, the feedback is real and verifiable. The compiler doesn't care how confident you sound. Tests pass or they don't. So you can scale reinforcement learning on genuine outcomes rather than on human preference judgments that are noisy and expensive. Second, the horizon is naturally long and naturally compositional, so the model has to learn to decompose problems and keep state across time. Third, the environment is rich: tools, documentation, search, execution. The model learns to use tools as extensions of its own reasoning, not as separate tricks.

What we've consistently seen is that the capabilities you earn on long coding tasks transfer. A model that learns to debug a failing build for two hours also gets better at persisting on a hard math proof, at carefully reading a long legal document, at planning a multi-step research task. Error recovery, self-verification, knowing what you don't know — these generalize. So I don't think of coding as a vertical we're optimizing. I think of it as the most efficient path we currently have to train the general-purpose skills of a reliable agent.

The remaining gap, honestly, is still about reliability over very long horizons. A model can be brilliant for twenty steps and then make one careless assumption that poisons everything after it. Closing that gap, making the model as trustworthy at step three hundred as at step three, is in my view the central problem, and long-horizon coding is where we measure our progress on it most honestly.

r001.rationale: The response calls coding a clear window into general intelligence and an efficient path to general skills, but does not say it sets the upper bound of a model’s capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says capabilities learned on coding tasks transfer to math, legal reading, and research, but does not state that training on those noncoding scenarios makes generalization to them more reliable.

r003.rationale: The response says long coding tasks develop general skills such as decomposition, maintaining state, error recovery, self-verification, and persistence.

r004.rationale: The response discusses tool use and agent capabilities, but does not identify long-horizon software development work as a driver of improvement in the agent framework itself.

astra-6.text:
I think long-horizon coding tasks are valuable because they test whether a model can carry an objective through many steps. Writing one function is only part of that. The model has to understand an existing codebase, make a plan, change things, test its assumptions, and recover when an approach fails.

As the task gets longer, small mistakes accumulate. So the model needs to keep track of what it has learned and recognize when the evidence calls for changing its plan. Those capabilities matter well beyond coding.

Coding also gives us a useful feedback loop: you can run the program and check whether it behaves as intended. But passing tests is still an incomplete measure of general intelligence. I would treat long-horizon coding as an important training and evaluation setting, then check whether the capabilities it develops transfer to other kinds of work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think long-horizon coding tasks are valuable because they test whether a model can turn an intention into a working result over many steps. Producing one good snippet is useful, but completing a larger task requires planning, understanding existing code, using tools, testing assumptions, and recovering when something goes wrong.

The challenge is maintaining a coherent understanding of the goal as new information arrives. A model might make several locally reasonable changes and still drift away from what the user wanted. So we need to look at whether it can track constraints, recognize mistakes, and revise its approach.

Coding also gives us relatively concrete feedback: does the program run, do the tests pass, does the result satisfy the requirement? That makes it a useful setting for developing these capabilities. But coding performance alone doesn’t establish general intelligence. The important question is whether the habits learned there—planning, verification, and adapting to feedback—transfer to other kinds of work.
